summary: Specifies Mobile IPv6, which lets nodes remain reachable while moving. Each mobile node keeps a home address and uses a care-of address at its current location, and packets sent to the home address are routed on. It was replaced by RFC 6275.

eli5.summary: Like mail forwarding when you move house: people still write your old address, and the post office sends it to where you are now.

questions: what is a home agent in mobile ipv6
what is route optimization in mobile ipv6
subtitle: How an IPv6 node keeps its address and its connections alive while it moves from one network to another.

tldr.problem: When an IPv6 node moves to a new link, packets sent to its old address no longer reach it, and changing the address would break transport and higher-layer connections.
tldr.mechanism: Each mobile node keeps a permanent home address and registers its current care-of address with a home agent on its home link. The home agent tunnels packets to the care-of address, and a correspondent node that learns the binding can send straight to it.
tldr.outcome: This RFC was replaced by RFC 6275, so new work should follow that document. It remains the original specification of Mobile IPv6 and its return routability procedure.

today: RFC 3775 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 6275, which is now the current Mobile IPv6 specification. It relies on a companion document, RFC 3776, for using IPsec between mobile nodes and home agents.

sections.title: The Problem of Moving in IPv6
sections.content:
Without specific support for mobility, packets destined to a mobile node would not reach it while it is away from its home link. The node could change its IP address every time it moves, but then it could not maintain transport and higher-layer connections when it changes location.

Mobile IPv6 lets a mobile node move from one link to another without changing its home address. Movement is then transparent to transport protocols and applications. The protocol works as well across similar media (one Ethernet segment to another) as across different media (Ethernet to a wireless LAN cell).

The RFC is explicit about its limits. It solves network-layer mobility management and does not try to solve links with unidirectional connectivity, access control on a visited link, local or hierarchical mobility management, assistance for adaptive applications, mobile routers, service discovery, or telling bit-error loss from congestion loss.

Compared with Mobile IP for IPv4, it needs no special foreign agent routers, makes route optimization a fundamental part of the protocol, uses IPv6 Neighbor Discovery instead of ARP, and uses a routing header rather than encapsulation for most packets sent to a mobile node away from home.
sections.eli5: If you change your phone number every time you move, your friends lose you. This protocol lets you keep one permanent address no matter where you are.

sections.title: Home Addresses, Care-of Addresses and Bindings
sections.content:
The home address is a unicast routable address assigned to the mobile node within its home subnet prefix on its home link. It is the node's permanent address, and ordinary IP routing delivers packets for it to the home link.

While the node is on a foreign link it also has one or more care-of addresses, which carry the subnet prefix of that foreign link. It can get them through normal IPv6 mechanisms such as stateless or stateful autoconfiguration. The one registered with the home agent is the primary care-of address.

The association of a home address with a care-of address, plus the remaining lifetime of that association, is a binding. The mobile node registers it by sending a Binding Update to a router on its home link, the home agent, and the home agent answers with a Binding Acknowledgement. Any node talking to the mobile node is a correspondent node, and it may itself be stationary or mobile.

Nodes track this state in three conceptual structures: the Binding Cache (kept by home agents and correspondent nodes), the Binding Update List (kept by each mobile node) and the Home Agents List (kept by home agents). Home and care-of addresses MUST be unicast routable addresses, and site-local addresses SHOULD NOT be used for either.
sections.eli5: Your home address is your permanent street address. A care-of address is the hotel you are staying at this week. The binding is the note you leave telling the post office which hotel to use.

sections.title: Two Ways to Reach a Mobile Node
sections.content:
The RFC describes two modes of communication between a mobile node and a correspondent node.

Bidirectional tunneling needs no Mobile IPv6 support in the correspondent node. The home agent uses proxy Neighbor Discovery to intercept packets addressed to the mobile node's home address on the home link, then tunnels each one to the primary care-of address using IPv6 encapsulation. In the other direction the mobile node reverse tunnels its packets to the home agent, which routes them normally.

Route optimization requires the mobile node to register its binding at the correspondent node. Before sending any packet, the correspondent node checks its cached bindings. If it finds one, it sets the IPv6 destination to the care-of address and adds a type 2 routing header carrying the home address. Packets then take the shortest path, congestion at the home agent and home link is avoided, and the effect of a home agent failure is reduced.

In the reverse direction the mobile node puts its care-of address in the IPv6 source address and its home address in a Home Address destination option. That keeps the care-of address transparent above the network layer, and lets packets pass through routers that do ingress filtering.
sections.eli5: The slow way is that all your mail goes to your old house first and is then forwarded. The fast way is that your friends learn your new address and write to it directly.

sections.title: The Mobility Header and Its Messages
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 adds a new IPv6 protocol, the Mobility Header, identified by Next Header value 135. It carries all messages for creating and managing bindings. Its fixed fields are Payload Proto, Header Len, MH Type, Reserved and a 16-bit Checksum, followed by message data and optional mobility options. The total length MUST be a multiple of 8 octets. Implementations SHOULD set Payload Proto to IPPROTO_NONE (59 decimal).

The Binding Update (type 5) tells another node about a new care-of address. Its flags are A (acknowledge), H (home registration), L (link-local address compatibility) and K (key management mobility capability). The Lifetime is counted in time units of 4 seconds, and a Lifetime of zero means the binding is deleted. The 16-bit Sequence # lets the receiver order updates; comparison is done modulo 65536.

The Binding Acknowledgement (type 6) carries a Status byte. Values below 128 mean the update was accepted; 128 and above mean it was rejected. Examples are 0 (accepted), 1 (accepted but prefix discovery necessary), 135 (sequence number out of window) and 136 to 138 (expired home nonce index, care-of nonce index, or both).

A correspondent node uses the Binding Refresh Request (type 0) to ask a mobile node to renew a binding, and the Binding Error (type 7) to report problems such as a Home Address option with no matching binding (status 1) or an unrecognized MH Type (status 2). The four Home Test Init, Care-of Test Init, Home Test and Care-of Test messages are used for return routability, described below.
sections.eli5: All the notes between you, the post office helper and your friends use one standard envelope. Inside, a number says whether it is a change-of-address, a thank-you, a reminder or an error report.

sections.title: Options, the Home Address Option and the Routing Header
sections.content:
Mobility messages can carry mobility options in type-length-value form. Receivers MUST silently ignore options they do not understand. The defined options are Pad1 (0), PadN (1), Binding Refresh Advice (2), Alternate Care-of Address (3), Nonce Indices (4) and Binding Authorization Data (5). The Binding Authorization Data option MUST be the last option and MUST NOT have trailing padding.

Two other pieces change how ordinary payload packets look. The Home Address destination option has Option Type 201 (0xC9) and Option Length 16. A mobile node away from home puts its home address there so the receiver can treat that address as the true source. Receiving it affects only that packet and creates no state.

The type 2 routing header lets a correspondent route a packet to the care-of address, with the home address as the final destination. It carries exactly one address, with Hdr Ext Len 2 and Segments Left 1. It uses a different routing type from regular source routing, so firewalls can apply different rules to it. A node MUST verify that the address inside is its own home address, and the header MUST NOT be automatically reversed for replies.
sections.eli5: The home address option is a sticker on your outgoing mail that says your permanent address. The routing header is a sticker on incoming mail that says to deliver it to your hotel, then to your home name.

sections.title: Return Routability: Proving a Mobile Node Is Where It Says
sections.content:
Binding Updates to a home agent are protected by an IPsec security association: both sides MUST support, and SHOULD use, ESP in transport mode with a non-NULL authentication algorithm. A correspondent node has no such pre-arranged relationship, so the RFC uses the return routability procedure. It gives the correspondent node reasonable assurance that the mobile node can receive packets at both its home address and its claimed care-of address.

The mobile node sends a Home Test Init through the home agent and a Care-of Test Init directly, at the same time. Each carries a 64-bit cookie. The correspondent replies with a Home Test (via the home agent) and a Care-of Test (directly). Each reply returns the cookie plus a 64-bit keygen token and a nonce index.

A token is the first 64 bits of HMAC_SHA1 over the relevant address, a nonce and a one-octet constant, keyed with the correspondent's 20-octet secret node key. The mobile node combines both tokens into the binding management key: Kbm = SHA1(home keygen token | care-of keygen token). It then sends a Binding Update with a Nonce Indices option and an authenticator that is the first 96 bits of an HMAC_SHA1 keyed with Kbm.

The correspondent keeps no per-mobile state until a valid Binding Update arrives, because it can recompute the tokens from the addresses and nonce indices. Nonces are kept for no more than MAX_NONCE_LIFETIME (240 seconds), tokens may be used for MAX_TOKEN_LIFETIME (210 seconds), and a binding set up this way MUST NOT exceed MAX_RR_BINDING_LIFETIME (420 seconds).
sections.eli5: To prove you really live at both your home and your hotel, a friend sends one secret half-code to each place. Only someone who gets both halves can put the code together and sign the change-of-address note.

sections.title: How Home Agents and Mobile Nodes Behave
sections.content:
To register, a mobile node sends the home agent a Binding Update with the H and A bits set, a Home Address option, and an Alternate Care-of Address option. If the home agent accepts, it creates a Binding Cache entry marked as a home registration and, unless it already has a binding, runs Duplicate Address Detection on the home link before acknowledging. It then multicasts a Neighbor Advertisement for the home address and answers Neighbor Solicitations as a proxy, so traffic for the mobile node arrives at the home agent and is tunneled onward. The Binding Acknowledgement is returned regardless of the A bit.

A mobile node detects an L3 handover mainly with Neighbor Unreachability Detection and Router Discovery. It then forms a new primary care-of address, registers it with the home agent, and afterwards updates correspondent nodes it is doing route optimization with. It SHOULD keep accepting packets at its previous care-of address to help smooth handovers, and it MUST NOT send Binding Updates about a new care-of address to its home agent more than MAX_UPDATE_RATE (3) times within a second.

When it returns home, the mobile node sends a Binding Update to the home agent with A and H set, Lifetime zero, and its home address as the care-of address. The home agent then deletes the binding and stops intercepting packets.

If the mobile node does not know a home agent address, it can send a Home Agent Address Discovery Request to the Home-Agents anycast address of its home subnet prefix, and the reply lists the home agents. Retransmissions use exponential back-off from one second up to MAX_BINDACK_TIMEOUT of 32 seconds, and retransmitted Binding Updates MUST use a greater Sequence Number.
sections.eli5: When you move, you tell your helper at home where you are. The helper then answers the door for you and forwards everything. When you come home, you tell the helper to stop.

sections.title: Threats and Protections
sections.content:
Most threats concern false bindings, usually leading to denial of service, and some also enable man-in-the-middle, hijacking, confidentiality or impersonation attacks. One example is a malicious node registering a victim's address as its care-of address, luring a correspondent into sending a large stream of data to the victim.

The protections are reverse tunneling as a mandatory feature, IPsec protection of Binding Updates to home agents, return routability for correspondent nodes, restrictions on the Home Address option (the receiver needs a Binding Cache entry for the home address) and a dedicated routing header type that avoids the vulnerabilities of regular routing headers.

The RFC says return routability defends against attackers who cannot monitor the path between the home agent and the correspondent node, and that attackers on that path could already attack without Mobile IPv6. It limits the lifetime of bindings so an attacker cannot leave a binding behind for long. Correspondent nodes stay stateless until an authorized Binding Update arrives, and all implementations MUST be able to administratively disable route optimization. With manual IPsec keying, the RFC notes the 16-bit sequence number space could cycle, roughly 455 days for a node moving every 10 minutes.
sections.eli5: The main worry is a stranger lying and saying you moved, so your mail goes to them. The rules make sure only someone who can really receive mail at both places can change your address.

sections.title: Assigned Numbers
sections.content:
The IANA section assigns protocol number 135 to the Mobility Header and creates three registries: Mobility Header types (0 to 7), Mobility Options (0 to 5) and Binding Acknowledgement Status Codes. New values can be allocated by Standards Action or IESG Approval.

The Home Address option is Option Type 0xC9 and the type 2 routing header value is 2. Four ICMPv6 message types are defined from the informational range: Home Agent Address Discovery Request (144) and Reply (145), and Mobile Prefix Solicitation (146) and Advertisement (147), which are used in lieu of Router Solicitations and Advertisements while the mobile node is away from the home link. Two Neighbor Discovery options are added: Advertisement Interval and Home Agent Information (type 8).
sections.eli5: Like giving each kind of note its own official number so everyone in the world uses the same ones.

fields.desc: Orders Binding Updates and matches the acknowledgement.

fields.desc: Home Registration: ask the receiver to act as home agent.

fields.desc: Sent as zero, ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: Remaining time in units of 4 seconds; zero deletes the binding.

items.desc: Asks a mobile node to renew its binding.

items.desc: Starts the home half of return routability.

items.desc: Starts the care-of half of return routability.

items.desc: Returns the home keygen token.

items.desc: Returns the care-of keygen token.

items.desc: Announces a new care-of address.

items.desc: Rejected without a stated reason.

items.desc: Rejected by policy.

items.desc: Receiver lacks resources.

items.desc: Home address is not on the home agent's link.

items.desc: No home registration exists.

items.label: Duplicate Address Detection failed
items.desc: Another node uses the home address.

items.label: Sequence number out of window
items.desc: The Sequence # was not greater than the last accepted.

items.label: Expired home nonce index
items.desc: The home nonce is no longer recognized.

items.desc: The care-of nonce is no longer recognized.

items.label: Expired nonces
items.desc: Both nonces are no longer recognized.

items.label: Registration type change disallowed
items.desc: The H bit differs from the existing binding.
